newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance crisis claims new victim -- car sales.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance crisis claims new victim -- car sales.

text.p: Thailand's recent finance sector crisis appears to have a new victim -- the auto industry.
The Thai car market is expected to grow at a slower pace than originally projected this year due to cautious lending for high-risk car purchases, industry analysts said.
The number of cars sold in February dipped 22 percent to 38,719 units from 49,503 the same month a year ago, according to the country's dominant auto group, Toyota Motor (Thailand).
Cumulative car sales in the first two months of the year declined 8.1 percent to 81,694 units compared with 88,872 in the same period last year.

"It's quite a big drop for February's car sales. Finance companies are toughening up new car loans due to their liquidity problem," Surapong Phasitpatnapong, spokesman for the Thai Automotive Industry Association, told Reuters.
"If the situation continues this way, there is a high possibility that the number of car sales this year would not reach 600,000 units," he said.
The association earlier this year projected total car sales in 1997 would reach 600,000 units compared with about 590,000 in 1996.
Finance firms have been reluctant to extend loans for any new car purchases since being hit by a liquidity crisis early this year, Surapong said.
"They may need to reserve their funds to meet possible withdrawals of their depositors," Surapong said.
On March 3, the central Bank of Thailand said it had ordered 10 cash-strapped finance companies to raise capital to assure creditors that they could continue operating soundly.
The announcement sparked a public run on deposits at many other finance companies.

"All finance companies are trimming down their exposure to (car) hire purchase loans," said an analyst at United Securities. "The loan is considered by the central bank as a high-risk lending activity and non-productive to the economy."
Analysts said more than 60 percent of car purchases are traditionally financed by hire purchase loans from finance companies.

"The association plans to discuss the strict regulations for the car loans with the finance companies," Ninnart Chaithirapinyo, senior managing director at Toyota Motor (Thailand), a unit of Toyota Motor Corp.
Toyota has the largest slice, or about 34 percent, of Thailand's car market, but faces competition from local units of Japan's Honda Motor Co Ltd and Mitsubishi Motors Corp.
The sluggish economy also reduced demand for cars, especially commercial vehicles whose sales have been closely in line with the country's economic growth, Surapong said.
The Bank of Thailand has forecast gross domestic product will grow by 6.8 percent this year against 6.7 percent a year ago, but private economists expect growth to be much lower.
